extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, economists, and policymakers studying patent value and empirical patent policy
extracted.subtask_short: estimating patent value via examiner lottery
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical strategy and data rules for identifying the incremental economic value of patent grants to startups by exploiting quasi-random assignment of applications to patent examiners with varying leniency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners assess if the claims in the application meet the legal thresholds of novelty, usefulness, and non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the legal thresholds the USPTO examiner evaluates when making first-action and final decisions; they form the substantive standard for granting patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of patent value (incremental value)
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a patent is the incremental economic benefit accruing to its holder from the legal right to exclude others from exploiting the invention, beyond what would be earned if the invention were not granted a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical analyses must separate this incremental value (the effect of exclusion rights) from the underlying economic value of the invention itself; failure to do so conflates invention quality with patent-right effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification strategy — quasi-random assignment and examiner leniency
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit the quasi-random assignment of applications to examiners combined with systematic variation in examiners' propensity to approve applications (leniency) to instrument for patent grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity rests on two features: (1) assignment to examiners is orthogonal to application quality conditional on controls; (2) examiners differ persistently in approval rates. Use this 'lottery' to isolate causal effects of patent grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of examiner leniency (instrument construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure examiner leniency as the approval rate of examiner j (number granted divided by number reviewed) prior to the application date, excluding the current application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include the focal application in the numerator/denominator. Exclude examiners with fewer than 10 prior reviews to ensure accuracy. Robustness: alternative constructions include leave-one-out estimators or using only the last three years of an examiner's history.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-stage strength and weak-instrument diagnostics
rubrics_metrics.description: Instrument relevance must be empirically strong (first-stage F-statistics well above rule-of-thumb of 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Kleibergen-Paap / F statistics. Example result: each percentage-point increase in an examiner’s prior approval rate leads to a 0.67 percentage-point increase in approval probability; moving from 25th to 75th percentile raises approval probability by ~11.8pp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of start date for measuring firm outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the USPTO first-action date (the examiner's first-action decision) as the starting point for measuring firm outcomes, not the filing date or final-decision date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: filing date has no resolution of uncertainty; final decision timing is endogenous (applicant responses affect timing). First-action resolves substantial uncertainty and is less subject to endogenous timing bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Startup sample definition and eligibility filters
rubrics_metrics.description: Define startups as incorporated U.S. applicants that are stand-alone for-profit firms (exclude not-for-profits, universities, government labs), not listed and not subsidiaries, qualifying for USPTO small-entity reduced fees, and with no patenting history in the previous 25 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also restrict to applicants for whom the USPTO records applicant identity (post-2001 applications) and exclude applicants acquired between filing and first-action. The paper's final sample: first-time patent applicants filed since 2001 with first-action by end-2009 and final decision by end-2013.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample time-window and censoring criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict sample to applications filed since 2001 (post-AIPA public disclosure of applicant identity) and require first-action by Dec 31, 2009 and final decision by Dec 31, 2013 to allow sufficient outcome follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These timing cutoffs ensure availability of applicant identity and enough post-decision years to measure longer-run employment, sales, innovation, and financing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome metrics for patent value
rubrics_metrics.description: Five types of outcome variables: (i) growth in sales and employment; (ii) follow-on patenting and patent citations; (iii) pledging patent applications as collateral to raise debt; (iv) venture funding (VC rounds); (v) fundraising via IPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NETS for employment and sales, USPTO patent and assignment databases for follow-on patents and pledges, VentureXpert for VC funding, and SDC (Thomson-Reuters) for IPOs. Report effects over multiple horizons (1–5 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching and data quality procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Match patent assignees to firm outcome datasets (e.g., NETS) using fuzzy matching algorithms supplemented with manual verification, name-change and location move checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually verify potential matches; report match rates (example: 80.01% match to NETS). Exclude unmatched startups when analyzing outcomes that rely on a particular data source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical specification, fixed effects, and standard errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate panel regressions / 2SLS with art-unit-by-application-year fixed effects, headquarter-state fixed effects, and cluster standard errors at the art-unit level; use linear probability model in first stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art-unit-by-year FE control for fine-grained time-varying demand/technology shocks. Cluster at art unit to allow arbitrary within-art-unit error correlation. Linear first-stage avoids introducing probit nonlinearity as identifying information; conclusions robust to probit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats to identification and validation checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Threats include non-random assignment (assignment correlated with application/applicant/examiner characteristics) and violation of the exclusion restriction (leniency affecting outcomes other than through patent grant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address via institutional arguments about assignment rules, implement validation tests (e.g., Righi and Simcoe 2017), test correlations between examiner leniency and observed drivers of success, and perform robustness checks (alternative instrument codings, excluding singletons, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of art-unit-by-year singletons
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications belonging to art-unit-by-year singletons do not contribute to identification and are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because fixed effects absorb the variation for singletons, they cannot be used to estimate treatment effects under the chosen FE structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'first application' for the firm
rubrics_metrics.description: The firm's 'first application' is defined as the first application the USPTO rules on (which in ~8% of cases may not be the firm's chronologically first-ever application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about this operational definition when constructing the sample and interpreting 'first-patent' effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion rules for examiners with sparse histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude examiners with fewer than 10 prior reviews when computing prior approval rates to ensure the instrument is based on sufficient data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results are robust to alternative cutoffs, but sparse-examiner approval rates may be noisy and distort instrument validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for review speed endogeneity (instrument for review speed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review speed (time to first-action) may be endogenous; instrument review speed using administrative delays: time from filing to assignment to examiner docket plus the examiner's average past docket-to-first-action time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including this instrument helps remove confounding if lenient examiners are also faster and review speed independently affects outcomes; use Kleibergen-Paap / F diagnostics for instrument strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish effects of first vs subsequent patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate effects separately for first, second, and third patent approvals because the value of patent grants may vary over time (first patent often has larger growth/financing effects than subsequent patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform subgroup and dynamic analyses; the paper finds strong effects for first patent grants and much weaker or no significant growth effects for subsequent patents, though subsequent patents still increase follow-on patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data source completeness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Public datasets often miss rejected or abandoned applications; internal USPTO databases are needed to observe the complete population of approved and rejected applications (especially for pre-2001 rejected apps and abandoned apps prior to public disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about limitations of public sources (e.g., PAIR lacks some rejected/abandoned apps) and justify access to internal USPTO data if using rejected-applications to identify incremental patent-right effects.
